stories.headline: Oil falls as Iran and Qatar hold a third day of talks to end the war
stories.what_happened: Iranian and Qatari officials held a third straight day of talks aimed at a deal to end the war, and oil prices fell on Monday. No deal has been reported.
stories.why_it_matters: A fifth of the world's oil normally passes through the Strait of Hormuz, so news from the talks moves fuel prices around the world.

key_facts.fact: Iranian and Qatari officials held a third straight day of talks aimed at a deal to end the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday the talks were "ongoing and progressing" and that Tehran is prepared for "both defence and diplomacy."
Brent crude ended October at its highest level in six months; the AP reported it fell about 7.5% on Monday to roughly $104.98 a barrel, against near $70 before the war.
Brent was about US$111 a barrel on Monday afternoon in Australia, after reaching US$117.64 earlier; it rose almost 14% in October.
Attacks on oil tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz are raising global energy and shipping costs.
OPEC+ kept December production targets steady on Sunday and is not expected to make further policy changes until next year.
An analyst, Tim Waterer, said rhetoric around Iran could rise and push Brent toward $120 after the US midterm elections.
The U.S.-Iran war is in its ninth month, and rising gas prices have been a major midterm issue.

stories.geography: Strait of Hormuz (between Iran and Oman); Qatar mediating; Iran; Saudi Arabia

sources.title: Oil slips more than 1% as talks continue on ending Iran war

stories.headline: Russian bombs kill at least 24 people waiting for aid in Zaporizhzhia region
stories.what_happened: A Russian attack on the Komyshuvakha settlement in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region killed at least 24 people on Monday, Ukraine's emergency service said. President Zelenskyy said it dampened hopes raised by a short truce nearby.
stories.why_it_matters: The attack came just after a six-day local truce and ahead of possible new talks, and shows how fragile hopes for peace are.

key_facts.fact: Ukraine's State Emergency Service said at least 24 people were killed, including two rescue workers and four police officers.

Regional governor Ivan Fedorov said Russian forces fired at least nine KAB-3000 bombs over the course of the day; the target was reportedly a school used for humanitarian purposes where people were receiving aid.
Zelenskyy called the attack "utterly horrific" and said Russia was sending "an entirely opposite signal" to hopes of progress toward peace.
Evacuees from occupied Oleshky arrived in Ukraine on Saturday via Belarus during a rare humanitarian truce between Kyiv and Moscow.

stories.geography: Komyshuvakha, Zaporizhzhia region, southeastern Ukraine; Oleshky, Kherson region

stories.headline: A six-day truce in Oleshky ends as Ukraine, Russia and the US eye talks next week
stories.what_happened: A six-day humanitarian ceasefire in Oleshky, in Russian-held Kherson region, ended on 1 November. Zelensky said three-way technical talks could be held 6-10 November, with Abu Dhabi the main venue under consideration.
stories.why_it_matters: Local truces and talks are small steps in a war that has gone on for years; where and when talks happen decides whether they can begin.

key_facts.fact: The 6-day ceasefire in Oleshky took effect on 27 October and officially ended on 1 November at 10:59 PM; it was meant for humanitarian aid and civilian evacuation.

Zelensky said technical-level talks among Ukraine, Russia and the US, with the US mediating, could be held 6-10 November 2026; Abu Dhabi is the main venue under consideration, with Switzerland also mentioned, and neither date nor venue is final.

Ukraine's General Staff said Russian forces used the pause to rotate personnel and bring in ammunition; Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Moscow had no detailed information and that moving troops during a ceasefire could be normal.
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Putin would take a call from Zelensky if Ukraine initiated it.

stories.geography: Oleshky, Kherson region (Russian-held); Abu Dhabi, UAE; Switzerland

stories.headline: WHO chief says Ebola shows the world must finish its pandemic treaty
stories.what_happened: WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus told a meeting in Geneva on Monday that recent outbreaks, including Ebola, show the pandemic treaty must be completed.
stories.why_it_matters: The treaty is meant to make sure vaccines and treatments reach every country fairly in a future outbreak.

key_facts.fact: Tedros said at a negotiating meeting in Geneva: "A pathogen threat anywhere can become a threat everywhere, to people of every country."
The Pandemic Agreement was adopted in May 2025 as a framework for future pandemics, but wealthy and developing nations still disagree on how it will work in practice.

Negotiators left out how the Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing (PABS) system will work; it governs how pathogens with pandemic potential are obtained and how resulting vaccines, tests and treatments are shared.
Tedros said that during COVID-19 vaccines were developed quickly, but many countries waited while others secured far more than they needed.

stories.geography: Geneva, Switzerland (WHO); Democratic Republic of Congo (Ebola outbreak)

stories.headline: Americans vote tomorrow in midterm elections that decide control of Congress
stories.what_happened: On the eve of the 3 November midterms, both parties made a final push. Trump gave a closing speech at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, and gas prices, the Iran war and the cost of living were central issues.
stories.why_it_matters: The elections decide who controls the House and Senate for the last two years of Trump's term.

key_facts.fact: AP's analysis says midterms usually act as referendums on the president's party; high gas prices, grocery costs and inflation have made that harder for Republicans.

Trump held rallies on Sunday in Iowa and Kansas and gave a nearly hourlong closing speech on Monday at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, saying Tuesday's elections could be the most important midterms in his lifetime.
Trump acknowledged that sitting presidents usually lose midterms, and said he hopes voters weigh falling oil prices when they vote.
Democrats could gain at least one chamber of Congress, which would give them subpoena power.
The administration pledged $15 billion to farmers before the midterms to offset diesel and fertilizer costs, with over half a one-time diesel payment.

Flooding in Pagosa Springs, Colorado, changed voting plans: affected residents can get replacement ballots at any voter center in the state, and mail ballots can be returned to any drop box or voter center by 7 p.m. on Election Day.
Voters in Washington, D.C., which has nearly 700,000 residents, more than Wyoming or Vermont, will elect a nonvoting House delegate and "shadow" senators and a representative who push for statehood.
Shane Dunn, 65, a former cook from Levittown, Pennsylvania, voted for the first time in his life.

stories.geography: United States; Washington D.C.; Iowa, Kansas, Colorado, Michigan

stories.headline: A court fight over 20,000 California mail ballots reaches the Supreme Court
stories.what_happened: The Trump administration asked the US Supreme Court on Monday for emergency relief over about 20,000 California mail ballots it suspects came from non-citizens. A judge and an appeals court had already refused.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how courts are settling disputes over who may vote, right at the end of an election.

key_facts.fact: The Trump administration asked the U.S. Supreme Court on Monday for emergency relief to set aside about 20,000 California mail ballots until the voters' status is verified.
An appeals court rejected the request, and U.S. District Chief Judge James Boasberg denied it and warned it could disenfranchise citizens.
California officials call the list highly unreliable and say it likely includes many U.S. citizens; a group said over 40% of people on it don't appear in the state voter file.
The Justice Department defended the list's accuracy.

sources.title: The Latest: final push before midterm elections

key_facts.fact: On Friday the S&P 500 fell 1.8%, the Dow 1.1% and the Nasdaq 2.9%; the Nasdaq was almost 8% below its record high from three weeks earlier.
More than US$2.6 trillion was wiped from big tech market value in October, and the Nasdaq fell about 6% for the month.

stories.headline: Hubble and Webb find 27 new icy bodies beyond Neptune
stories.what_happened: Using NASA's Hubble and James Webb telescopes together for the first time on these objects, astronomers found 27 previously unknown trans-Neptunian objects, the smallest about 3 miles (5 km) across.
stories.why_it_matters: These leftover building blocks keep clues about how planets formed.

key_facts.fact: The Hubble and Webb telescopes observed the same patch of sky at the same time; Hubble collected visible light and Webb infrared light.
The survey found 27 previously unknown trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs), small icy bodies beyond Neptune; the smallest is about 3 miles (5 km) across.
Most TNOs are more than 100 million times fainter than what the naked eye can see.

Cold TNOs formed where they now orbit, on nearly circular paths close to the plane of the planets; hot TNOs formed between the orbits of Uranus and Neptune and were scattered outward when the giant planets migrated early on.
Small TNOs have colors similar to much larger ones, suggesting their surfaces have changed little since the solar system formed.
TNOs are leftover building blocks that never grew into full planets, so they preserve clues about how planets formed.
Marielle Eduardo of the University of Victoria led the size study and Anastasia Morgan of Northern Arizona University led the color study; the papers are in The Astronomical Journal.

sources.title: NASA's Hubble and Webb discover ancient worlds that remember their past

stories.headline: Two NASA spacecraft will swing past Earth to fire their engines toward Mars
stories.what_happened: NASA's twin ESCAPADE spacecraft will each do a powered Earth flyby in November, on 7 and 9 November, to speed up toward Mars.
stories.why_it_matters: It uses Earth's gravity plus an engine burn to save fuel on the way to Mars.

key_facts.fact: Each spacecraft combines Earth's gravity with a roughly 9-minute engine burn at closest approach, raising speed by more than 1,000 mph, from about 6.3 to 6.7 miles per second.
Spacecraft 1's closest approach is around 5 a.m. EST on Saturday 7 November and spacecraft 2's around 6 a.m. EST on Monday 9 November.
At closest approach each is 600 to 1,100 miles above Earth and about the size of a standard refrigerator.

ESCAPADE launched in November 2025 when Earth and Mars were on opposite sides of the Sun; the spacecraft looped around the Earth-Sun L2 point and returned to use Earth's gravity once the planets realigned.
After a roughly 10-month cruise they arrive at Mars on 7 and 9 September 2027.
ESCAPADE will be the first multi-spacecraft mission to fly in formation around Mars, studying how the solar wind drives atmospheric loss.

stories.geography: Earth to Mars; burns over southern Australia

stories.headline: Before the UK-EU summit, Brussels and London disagree on how to get closer
stories.what_happened: The EU and UK hold a summit on 20 November. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the UK should first join EU defence frameworks, while UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the UK stays committed to closer defence cooperation.
stories.why_it_matters: The UK and EU are close neighbours and trade partners, so how they cooperate affects prices, jobs and security.

key_facts.fact: The EU and UK are holding a summit on 20 November; both sides agree on the need for closer cooperation but differ on how.
Kallas said the UK should first join the EU's existing defence frameworks rather than open talks on rejoining the bloc, and said: "These negotiations will be difficult, and we are not there yet."

Streeting said the UK is committed to closer defence cooperation even though it opted out of the EU's EUR150 billion SAFE defence loan scheme last year after talks failed over an estimated EUR4-6 billion entry fee.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to rebuild EU relations, including on trade, education, energy and defence, and has not ruled out talks on full EU membership.
Streeting warned against EU protectionism in the "Made in Europe" industrial drive, because the UK is outside the single market.

stories.headline: Belgium's prime minister offers his government's resignation after budget talks fail
stories.what_happened: Prime Minister Bart De Wever offered his government's resignation to King Philippe on Monday after overnight budget talks failed. The king is considering it and will consult party chairs from Tuesday.
stories.why_it_matters: Belgium must cut its deficit to meet EU rules; a government collapse could mean new elections.

key_facts.fact: De Wever met King Philippe on Monday 2 November to offer his government's resignation after talks with his core cabinet on the budget failed overnight.

The palace said the king is considering the resignation, will consult coalition party chairs from Tuesday 3 November, and says the country "cannot afford" a prolonged political crisis; De Wever is due to meet him again on Friday 6 November.
Belgium must save EUR10 billion to stay within EU spending limits; the 2025 deficit was 5% of GDP against an EU maximum of 3%.
Centrist and socialist parties want EUR1-1.5 billion raised by taxing higher incomes, while the conservative N-VA and liberal MR want spending cuts.

If confirmed, Yotova would be Bulgaria's first elected female head of state.
Yotova advocated a peaceful resolution to the war in Ukraine through negotiations with Russia, while Gyurov signalled closer alignment with Western partners.
The presidency is largely ceremonial, but the president leads the armed forces, can veto legislation and signs international treaties; presidents serve five-year terms, limited to two.

stories.headline: Russian bombs kill at least 24 people waiting for aid in Zaporizhzhia region
stories.what_happened: A Russian attack on the Komyshuvakha settlement in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region killed at least 24 people on Monday, Ukraine's emergency service said. President Zelenskyy said it dampened hopes raised by a short truce nearby.
stories.why_it_matters: The attack came just after a six-day local truce and ahead of possible new talks, and shows how fragile hopes for peace are.

key_facts.fact: Ukraine's State Emergency Service said at least 24 people were killed, including two rescue workers and four police officers.

Regional governor Ivan Fedorov said Russian forces fired at least nine KAB-3000 bombs over the course of the day; the target was reportedly a school used for humanitarian purposes where people were receiving aid.
Zelenskyy called the attack "utterly horrific" and said Russia was sending "an entirely opposite signal" to hopes of progress toward peace.
Evacuees from occupied Oleshky arrived in Ukraine on Saturday via Belarus during a rare humanitarian truce between Kyiv and Moscow.
